lines.speaker: narrator

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: Good morning, Kingfisher Removals, Jess speaking. How can I help you?

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: Oh, hello. I'm moving house next month and I'd like to get a quote, and maybe book a date if you've got anything free.

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: Of course. I'll just take a few details first. Can I have your name, please?

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: Yes, it's Martin Pelham.

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: Is that P-E-L-L-A-M?

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: Not quite. It's P-E-L-H-A-M. There's an H in the middle. People always miss it.

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: Sorry about that. Pelham, with an H. Got it. And where are you moving from at the moment?

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: I'm in a flat at 27 Tanner Street. That's T-A-N-N-E-R. It's in Bramford, just behind the railway station.

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: Lovely, I know it. Is there a lift in the building?

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: There is, but it's tiny, and I'm on the second floor, so I don't think your team will want to squeeze a sofa into it.

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: No, they'll probably use the stairs, then. Now, do you have a date in mind?

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: Well, originally we were going to move on Saturday the 9th of August, but the people buying our flat have asked for an extra week.

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: So that would make it the following Saturday?

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: Exactly, Saturday the 16th of August. Is that possible?

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: Let me have a look... yes, we've still got a team free that day, so I'll pencil you in. And how big is the place you're moving to?

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: It's a house this time. At the moment we've only got two bedrooms, but the new one has three, plus a small garden, so it'll be a lot more space.

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: Very nice. And are there any items we should know about? Anything particularly heavy or fragile?

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: Let me think. There's a grandfather clock that belonged to my grandmother. Oh, no, actually, my sister's taking that, so you won't need to worry about it. But there is an antique mirror. It's quite large and the frame's very delicate.

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: Okay, I'll make a note of the mirror, and the team will bring special padding for it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: So, Mr Pelham, based on what you've told me, the full price would be 640 pounds for the day. That includes the van, the fuel and three removal staff.

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: That sounds reasonable. Do I need to pay anything now?

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: Yes, there's a deposit to secure the date. It used to be 75 pounds, but it went up in April, so it's now 90 pounds. The rest is paid on the day of the move.

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: Fine. And is there anything I need to organise at my end?

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: Parking is the main thing. Our van is quite long, so it needs a space right outside the building. Is there a car park, or is it street parking on Tanner Street?

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: Street parking. I suppose I'd better ask my landlord about it?

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: Actually, your landlord can't help with the street, I'm afraid. You'll need a parking permit from the council. You can usually get one online, but do it at least a week before.

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: Right, I'll sort that out this week. Anything else?

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: Just one thing people often forget. Please defrost the freezer the day before, otherwise there's water all over the van. You don't need to empty the bookshelves, though. The team can box those up for you.

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: Good to know. What about boxes for everything else? Do I have to buy my own?

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: No, you get 20 cardboard boxes free with every booking, and a roll of tape. Bubble wrap isn't included, but we can sell you some if you need it.

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: I think I'll be okay for bubble wrap, thanks.

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: No problem. Last question, then. How did you hear about us? Was it our website?

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: No, not the website, though I did have a look at it afterwards. It was my neighbour, actually. She used you last year and said you were brilliant.

lines.speaker: receptionist
lines.text: Oh, that's lovely to hear. Right, I'll email you a booking confirmation this afternoon, with a link for paying the deposit.

lines.speaker: customer
lines.text: Brilliant. Thanks very much for your help.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

lines.text: Part 2. You will hear a volunteer coordinator talking to a group of new volunteers about a lantern festival. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: Kia ora, everyone, and thanks for coming along tonight. My name's Rob Fletcher and I'm the volunteer coordinator for this year's Riverbend Lantern Festival. It's great to see so many new faces. About half of you have never volunteered with us before, so I'll go through the basics, and then there'll be time for questions at the end.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: First, a bit of news you've probably already heard. After eleven years in the old Wharf Street car park, the festival is moving to Riverside Park. A lot of people have asked me why. Some think we were after a bigger crowd, but honestly, our numbers have been fine for years.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: And yes, the park is right on the main bus routes, which is great, but that's really just a bonus. The actual reason is that the car park has been sold, and the council's turning it into apartments, so we simply had to find a new home.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: Now, what to wear. We'd planned to give everyone a festival T-shirt this year, but unfortunately our supplier let us down and they won't arrive in time. So when you sign in, please pick up one of the yellow high-vis vests from the volunteer tent and keep it on all evening.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: What you wear underneath is up to you, but do bring a waterproof jacket of your own. We can't supply those, and it gets pretty cold and damp down by the river.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: On the day itself, that's Saturday the 14th of March, the gates open to the public at five. In previous years we've asked volunteers to come at four, but hanging all the lanterns along the new path takes longer than you'd think, so this year please be here by half past three.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: Right, one thing I want to be really clear about is lost children. With a big crowd in the dark, it happens every year. In the past, volunteers would walk the child over to the information tent, but we've found that parents usually go back to the spot where they last saw their child, so the child's no longer there.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: So this year, if you find a lost child, stay with them exactly where you are and call the safety team on your radio. They'll come to you. And please don't go to the main stage to ask for an announcement. That tends to cause more panic than it solves.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: Okay, now let me take you round the different areas of the festival, because there are a few changes you'll need to know about.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: Starting with the craft tent, where people make their own lanterns. Last year it was absolutely packed, and we did look into hiring a bigger tent, but the cost was just too high, so it's the same size as before. The real problem there is staffing. We've still only got four helpers for the whole evening, so if anyone's keen, please let me know.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: Next to it you'll find the food market. You won't remember it from previous years, because until now we've only ever had one coffee van. This is the first time we've had proper food stalls. Entry to the market's free, of course. The stallholders pay us a fee instead.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: Then there's the children's zone, on the grass beside the playground. Some parents think it's only for toddlers, but there are activities for kids of all ages. Because that part of the park isn't lit, though, it shuts at seven, a couple of hours before everything else.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: The main stage is at the far end of the park. It's got a roof, so even if it rains, the bands will keep playing. What has changed is the space in front of it. We've made the dance area twice as big as last year, so there's plenty of room for everyone.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: The riverside path is where the floating lanterns are released, and it's the highlight of the night. However, it's very exposed, so if the wind picks up, we'll have to close it for safety. We'll make that call on the night.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: And finally, the bike park by the north gate. We had one last year, so it's nothing new, but this year there's a charge of two dollars a bike, because we're paying security staff to keep an eye on it. All the money goes back into the festival.

lines.speaker: coordinator
lines.text: Right, that's everything from me for now. Grab yourselves a cup of tea, and then I'll take your questions.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

lines.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of blue pigments used in art. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Good morning, everyone. In this series we've been looking at the materials artists have used over the centuries, and today I want to focus on one colour in particular: blue. It might seem strange to give a whole lecture to a single colour, but blue has a surprisingly dramatic history.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Let's start with a simple question. Why is blue so rare in early art? You'll find plenty of reds, browns and yellows in cave paintings, for example, because those colours come from earth and clay, which are everywhere. Blue is a different story.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: There are blue plants, of course, and people did make dyes from them. The trouble is that, as paints, plant-based blues are unreliable. Leave them in strong light and they fade within a few years, sometimes within months. So for a very long time, a lasting blue was something painters could only dream of.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: The first real solution came from ancient Egypt, roughly four and a half thousand years ago. Egyptian craftsmen discovered that if they heated sand, lime and copper together at a very high temperature, they got a beautiful, stable blue. Some textbooks will tell you the key ingredient was bronze, and it's true that bronze scraps were sometimes used, but only because bronze contains copper. Copper is what gives the colour.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: What makes Egyptian blue so important is that it's generally considered the first synthetic pigment. In other words, it was the first colour that was manufactured rather than simply dug out of the ground. It was used for over three thousand years, right through the Roman period, and then, rather mysteriously, the recipe was forgotten.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: There's a lovely modern twist to this story. Egyptian blue has an unusual property: when light falls on it, it glows. Not in a way we can see, but in the infrared, which a special camera can pick up. So archaeologists can now photograph a statue that looks completely white, and tiny traces of blue paint suddenly light up on the screen.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Now, the second pigment I want to talk about is ultramarine, which many people consider the most beautiful blue of all. Ultramarine comes from a stone called lapis lazuli. For centuries, almost all of the lapis used in Europe came from a single group of mines in the mountains of what is now Afghanistan. The name 'ultramarine' actually means 'beyond the sea', which tells you how far it had to travel.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Turning the stone into paint was slow, difficult work, and so the pigment was extraordinarily expensive. In Renaissance Italy, the finest ultramarine could cost more than gold, weight for weight. Painters didn't usually buy it themselves. The wealthy clients who commissioned a painting would supply it, and their contracts often stated exactly how much was to be used.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Because of the cost, artists used it with great care. Rather than spreading it across the background, they usually saved it for the most important part of a picture, very often the cloak of the Virgin Mary, which is why she's so frequently shown dressed in blue. Less important areas, such as skies, were generally painted with cheaper blues.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Let's move forward to the early eighteenth century and to Berlin, where our third blue appeared. Prussian blue is unusual because nobody set out to make it. It was discovered entirely by accident, by a colour maker who was actually trying to produce a red. One of his ingredients had been contaminated, and instead of red, he got a deep blue.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Prussian blue was cheap and very strong, and it spread quickly, not just across Europe but as far as Japan. When it reached Japan in the nineteenth century, it was taken up enthusiastically by artists who made woodblock prints. Some of the most famous Japanese images of waves and mountains owe their intense blue to this accidental discovery in Germany.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: That brings us to our final blue. Even in the nineteenth century, real ultramarine was still too expensive for most painters. So in 1824, a French society that supported industry offered a prize to anyone who could find a cheap way of making it artificially. Within four years, a chemist had succeeded, and synthetic ultramarine was soon being produced in factories at a tiny fraction of the old price.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: This made blue available to everyone, from the Impressionists to people decorating their homes. And in a sense, it closes the circle: blue started out as one of the rarest colours in art and ended up as one of the most ordinary. Next week, we'll look at what happened when chemists turned their attention to purple.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

paragraphs.text: Long before electric air conditioning was invented, people living in the hot, dry regions of the Middle East had found a way to keep their homes cool without burning any fuel. Their solution was the windcatcher, a tall tower rising above the roof of a building and open near the top on one or more sides. Known in Persian as the badgir, the windcatcher became a defining feature of desert towns across Iran and the shores of the Persian Gulf. The central Iranian city of Yazd, where hundreds of these towers still stand, is often called the city of windcatchers. paragraphs.text: A windcatcher works by exploiting two simple physical principles. The first is the pressure of moving air. When the wind strikes the open side of a tower, the air is forced down a vertical shaft and into the rooms below. As this fresh air enters the house, it pushes warmer, stale air out through doors and windows on the opposite side. The second principle comes into play when there is no wind at all. Because warm air is lighter than cool air, it naturally rises. On still days, air that has been heated inside the house drifts up the tower and escapes from the top, drawing cooler air in at ground level to replace it. This process is known as the stack effect, and it means that a well-designed tower continues to ventilate a building even in calm weather.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Over the centuries, builders added several refinements to make the system more effective. Inside the tower, the shaft was usually divided by thin walls into a number of separate channels, so that air arriving from one direction could descend through one channel while warm air left through another. The towers themselves were generally built of thick mud brick, a material that absorbs heat slowly during the day and releases it at night. In some houses, the incoming air was led across a shallow pool or past porous clay jars filled with water. As the water evaporated, it absorbed heat from the air, lowering its temperature by several degrees. The most sophisticated designs connected the tower to a qanat, an underground channel that carried water from distant hills, so that air was cooled as it passed over the flowing water deep beneath the building.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The shape and height of windcatchers varied considerably from place to place. In areas where the wind blew mainly from one direction, a tower open on a single side was sufficient. Where the wind was less predictable, builders preferred towers with four or even eight openings, so that at least one would always face the breeze. Height mattered too. Air moves faster further above the ground and carries less dust, so taller towers delivered stronger and cleaner airflow. In wealthy households, the height and decoration of a windcatcher also served as a visible sign of the owner's status.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: During the twentieth century, many windcatchers fell into disrepair. Electric fans and, later, mechanical air conditioning offered a more convenient way to stay cool, and new buildings were rarely designed with towers. Yet mechanical cooling comes at a considerable cost. According to Dr Leila Farahani, an energy analyst at the Institute for Desert Architecture, air conditioning now accounts for a large share of summer electricity demand in many hot countries. The units themselves also release heat into the surrounding streets, which makes cities even warmer and increases the demand for cooling still further.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Concerns of this kind have led to renewed interest in the old technology. In 2019, an engineering team led by Professor Martin Okafor at the University of Carran fitted a modern windcatcher to a two-storey office building. Their tower was made of lightweight aluminium rather than brick, and its openings were fitted with movable louvres that a computer opened and closed according to the direction of the wind. Sensors measured the temperature inside the building, and whenever it rose too high, a fine mist of water was sprayed into the shaft to cool the incoming air. Over two summers, the team found that the building needed mechanical cooling on only a quarter of the days on which it would normally have been switched on.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Okafor admits that windcatchers are not suitable everywhere. They work best in dry climates, because evaporative cooling is far less effective when the air is already humid. They are also difficult to add to tall apartment blocks, where air would have to travel long distances through the building. Nevertheless, he believes that the principle behind the towers deserves far wider attention. 'For centuries, builders understood how to work with the climate rather than against it,' he says. 'Modern engineering has a great deal to learn from them.'

passage.title: The puzzle of the dawn chorus

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who wakes before sunrise in a temperate woodland in spring will hear it: a swelling wave of birdsong that begins in near-darkness, reaches a peak around first light and fades within an hour or two. The dawn chorus is one of the most familiar events in the natural world, yet it has proved surprisingly difficult to explain. Singing is not free. It consumes energy, it takes time that could otherwise be spent feeding, and it can reveal a bird's position to predators. Why, then, do so many species concentrate their most intense singing into the hour when they are hungriest after a long night without food? Over the past half-century, biologists have proposed a range of answers, and the debate is still far from settled.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the earliest explanations focused on the physics of sound. At dawn the air is usually cool and still, without the turbulence that develops later in the day as the sun heats the ground. In theory, these conditions should allow songs to travel further and remain clearer over distance. The ornithologist Harriet Vance, working in English beech woods in the 1970s, played recorded songs at different times of day and reported that a song broadcast at dawn could be detected up to twice as far away as the same song at midday. However, later studies in other habitats produced mixed results. Critics also pointed out that if sound transmission were the main factor, birds ought to sing just as intensely at dusk, when conditions are often similar. Few of them do.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second idea concerns food rather than sound. Many songbirds feed on insects, and in the dim light before sunrise their prey is both hard to see and relatively inactive in the cold. According to this view, argued most forcefully by the behavioural ecologist Tomás Ibarra, the early morning is simply a poor time to search for food, so a bird loses little by singing instead. Once the light improves and the air warms, it becomes more profitable to stop singing and start foraging. Ibarra points to his own observations of warblers in northern Spain, which suggest that the chorus ends almost exactly when the light becomes strong enough for efficient hunting.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other researchers regard the chorus as a form of advertisement. A small bird may lose up to a tenth of its body weight during a cold night, simply keeping warm. A male that sings vigorously at dawn is therefore demonstrating that he has come through the night with energy to spare, a message that rivals and potential mates cannot easily fake. Experiments by the Kessler Research Group in Austria appeared to support this idea: when wild great tits were given extra food the previous evening, they began singing earlier and sang for longer the next morning. Yet the same group noted that the effect was modest, and that birds which received no extra food still sang at length. Energy reserves, they concluded, are only part of the story.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A fourth explanation looks instead at the social lives of birds. In many species, a female lays her eggs early in the morning and is thought to be most fertile shortly afterwards. A male who sings loudly at this time may be guarding his partner, warning other males to keep away when the risk of a rival mating with her is greatest. The field biologist Ruth Adeyemi adds a further, territorial dimension. In her view, the chorus works as a kind of daily roll call: each male announces that he is still alive and still in possession of his territory. A male whose neighbour falls silent can quickly move to claim the vacant ground, so remaining quiet at dawn carries a real risk.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In recent years, towns and cities have provided researchers with an unplanned experiment. Street lighting means that urban birds experience something like daybreak long before the sun rises, and morning traffic noise can drown out songs once the rush hour begins. A study led by Dr Paolo Ricci in Milan found that blackbirds living near bright street lamps began their song up to an hour earlier than those in darker parks, and that birds in noisy districts started earlier still. For Ricci, the second finding suggests that birds are trying to be heard before traffic noise makes communication difficult, which supports the importance of sound transmission. The first, however, implies that timing is also linked to light levels, which fits Ibarra's argument. His conclusion is that the chorus is probably shaped by several pressures at once, and that their relative importance differs from one species to another.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In June 1991, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted, blasting millions of tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere. There the gas formed a fine haze of sulphate particles that reflected a small fraction of incoming sunlight back into space, and over the following year average global temperatures fell by roughly half a degree Celsius. For a number of scientists, the episode raised a tantalising possibility: if a volcano could cool the planet by accident, perhaps humans could do so deliberately. The proposal that grew out of this thought, known as stratospheric aerosol injection, would involve high-altitude aircraft releasing reflective particles into the upper atmosphere. Within two decades it has travelled from the fringes of climate science to the agendas of respected research bodies. That shift is understandable, but I shall argue that much of the enthusiasm surrounding it rests on a misunderstanding of what the technique can and cannot achieve.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The attraction is easy to see. Cutting greenhouse gas emissions is slow, expensive and politically fraught, and even if emissions stopped tomorrow, the carbon dioxide already in the atmosphere would go on warming the planet for decades. Aerosol injection, by contrast, promises results within months, at a cost that some estimates put at a few billion dollars a year, a trivial sum when set against the damage caused by heatwaves, droughts and failed harvests. The atmospheric physicist Daniel Moreau has gone so far as to call it 'the only lever we have that works on a human timescale'. It would be dishonest to dismiss this case out of hand. The speed and cheapness of the approach are real advantages, and anyone who opposes it must take them seriously.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that aerosols treat a symptom rather than the disease. They would lower temperatures, but they would do nothing to slow the build-up of carbon dioxide itself, nor to stop the oceans from growing more acidic as they absorb it, a change that threatens corals and shellfish however cool the water may be. Moreover, the particles drift out of the stratosphere within a year or two, so they would have to be replenished continuously, perhaps for a century or more. If injection were ever halted abruptly, whether because of war, economic collapse or political disagreement, the warming it had been masking would return within a few years, far faster than ecosystems or societies could adapt. Climate scientists call this 'termination shock', and in my view it is the most serious objection to the whole enterprise, because it would bind future generations to a programme they never chose.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second problem concerns fairness. Global average temperature is a convenient figure, but nobody actually lives in the global average. Simulations run at the Nordhavn Climate Centre suggest that reflecting sunlight would alter rainfall unevenly, possibly weakening the monsoons on which hundreds of millions of farmers in South Asia and West Africa depend. Other models are less pessimistic, and the honest answer is that no one yet knows. But that uncertainty is precisely the point. A technology whose regional effects cannot be predicted, and which a single wealthy nation could deploy on its own, raises questions of governance that existing international institutions are simply not equipped to answer.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Opponents frequently add a third argument, often described as 'moral hazard': the fear that the mere prospect of a technological fix will weaken the determination to cut emissions. I find this argument less convincing than its supporters suppose. Surveys conducted by the sociologist Ingrid Halvorsen found that members of the public who learned about geoengineering became, if anything, slightly more worried about climate change, not less. The real risk lies elsewhere. It is not ordinary citizens who are likely to relax, but governments and industries already searching for reasons to delay, who may seize on the idea as a convenient excuse. That is a political danger rather than a psychological one, and it must be met with political rather than scientific answers.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this means that research should stop. Some campaigners have called for an international ban not only on deployment but on outdoor experiments of any kind. This seems to me mistaken. If the climate warms faster than expected, future leaders may come under intense pressure to attempt aerosol injection, and it would be far better for them to decide on the basis of careful evidence than in a state of panic. Small, openly reported field trials, supervised by bodies that include representatives of the countries most at risk, would allow scientists to test their predictions without committing anyone to deployment.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What research must never become is an alibi. At best, solar geoengineering might buy time in which to cut emissions and draw carbon out of the air; it cannot replace either effort. Describing it as a form of insurance is reasonable only if we remember what insurance is for. It reduces the cost of a disaster, but it is no reason to drive more recklessly. The technology deserves careful study. It does not yet deserve our hopes.
